opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this started really as a side project, kind of a "what if" question that I couldn't stop thinking about. Game engines are these incredibly complex pieces of software. People spend years hand-writing the rules: physics, rendering, collision, game logic, all of it. And I was wondering, can a neural network just *learn* all of that by watching? Instead of writing the code that produces the frames, could you have a model that, given what happened so far and what the player is doing right now, simply predicts the next frame, and do it well enough and fast enough that you could actually play it?

What excited me was that it felt like a real test of whether these generative models understand the world they're producing. It's one thing to generate a nice-looking image or a short video clip. It's another to have something interactive, where the player is in control, and the model has to stay consistent over time. If you shoot something, the state has to change. If you walk around a corner and come back, things should still make sense. That turned out to be much harder and much more interesting than just making pretty pictures.

There was also a practical curiosity: could this run in real time? Diffusion models were known for being slow, needing many steps per image. So a big part of the fun was asking whether we could push it to the point where it feels like a game rather than a slideshow.

And honestly, more broadly, I was excited about what it might hint at for the future. If a model can learn to simulate a game, maybe eventually the way we create interactive experiences changes. Instead of programming everything explicitly, you could describe or demonstrate what you want, and the model handles the simulation. That felt like a glimpse of a pretty different paradigm, and I wanted to see how far we could get.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a neural network can learn a game engine’s rules and predict playable frames in real time, but it does not clearly specify simulating an existing game.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So this started as something Dani Valevski and I were playing with on the side, and the question we were really curious about was pretty simple: can a neural network be a game engine? Not render a frame, not generate a clip, but actually be the thing that runs the game in real time, where you hold a controller, you press a key, and the model produces the next frame based on your action and what came before.

What made it exciting was that it sat at the intersection of two things. On one side you have diffusion models, which had gotten remarkably good at producing images and video. On the other side you have game engines, which are these very deliberate, hand-written systems full of rules about physics, collision, state. And we wanted to see whether the generative side could absorb the rules side just by watching gameplay. Could it learn that when you walk into a wall you stop, that when you shoot an enemy its health goes down, that a door you opened stays open when you turn around and come back?

We picked DOOM because it's the canonical "can it run DOOM" thing, but also for practical reasons. It's simple enough that there's a lot of structure to learn, but complex enough that it's genuinely hard. There's state that persists, there's an inventory, there's a map. And it's a game that people know, so if something looked wrong, anyone could tell.

The part that I found most interesting to explore was the interactive loop. Generating video offline is one problem. Generating it frame by frame, conditioned on a human's actions, at a frame rate where it feels like a game, is a different problem. You have to deal with the model's own errors compounding over time, because it's always conditioning on frames it produced itself. So a lot of the fun was figuring out how to train an agent to play the game to collect data, how to make the model robust to its own drift, and then how to make it fast enough that you could actually sit down and play it.

And honestly, part of the excitement was just the vision underneath it. If a neural network can learn to be a game engine from gameplay footage, then you start to imagine a world where games, or interactive experiences more generally, aren't programmed line by line but are learned and generated. That felt like a question worth poking at.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a neural network can be the game engine and run a game in real time, then identifies DOOM as the game being explored.

astra-6.text: I was excited by the idea of a neural network being the game engine itself. Instead of writing explicit rules for how everything moves and interacts, could you have a model generate the next frame based on what the player does? That turns generation into something interactive: you take an action, the world responds, and the model has to keep that world coherent. I wanted to explore how far you could push that idea and whether it could actually feel like playing a game.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a neural network could act as the game engine and generate interactive frames, but it does not specify simulating an existing game in real time entirely with the network.

sol-6.1.text: I was excited to explore whether a neural network could learn to simulate an interactive world. Instead of explicitly programming the rules of a game, could we train a model to predict what happens next from what it sees and the actions a player takes? The interesting part was closing that loop—letting someone play, feeding the model’s output back into itself, and seeing whether it could keep producing a coherent experience.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a neural network can simulate an interactive world, but does not specify an existing game or real-time simulation.
